title: Contravariant finite representable matrices and signed total homotopies
statement:
Let $I$ be a small category and $\mathcal C$ an abelian category [def-sp-abelian], in compatible universes. Put $R_i(j)=\mathbf Z[\operatorname{Hom}_I(i,j)]$. Let $\mathcal F_I$ have objects finite lists $(i_1,\ldots,i_k)$, including the empty list, interpreted as $\bigoplus_{t=1}^kR_{i_t}$, and morphisms the natural transformations between these functors. For $X:I\to\operatorname{Ch}^{\geq0}(\mathcal C)$, there is an additive contravariant evaluation $E_X$ on $\mathcal F_I$. It sends a list to $\bigoplus_tX(i_t)$ and a map $R_i\to R_j$ determined at $i$ by $\sum_{\alpha:j\to i}c_\alpha[\alpha]$ to $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha X(\alpha):X(j)\to X(i)$. On finite sums it is the transposed matrix of these maps. This prescription is well-defined and preserves identities, sums and composition contravariantly, and it is natural in $X$.

For a nonnegative chain complex $P$ in $\mathcal F_I$, define $L_X(P)^{n,r}=E_X(P_n)^r$ for $n,r\geq0$, with $d_n=E_X(\partial_P)$ and internal differential $d_r$. Its total complex is
$$\mathbb T_X(P)^m=\bigoplus_{n+r=m}E_X(P_n)^r,\qquad d=d_n+(-1)^n d_r,$$
as in [def-sp-double-complex-total]. Every chain map $u:P\to Q$ gives a natural cochain map $\mathbb T_X(u):\mathbb T_X(Q)\to\mathbb T_X(P)$. If $u,v:P\to Q$ and $h_n:P_n\to Q_{n+1}$ satisfy $u-v=\partial_Qh+h\partial_P$, the evaluated components $E_X(h_n)^r:E_X(Q_{n+1})^r\to E_X(P_n)^r$ form a degree-minus-one total homotopy with
$$\mathbb T_X(u)-\mathbb T_X(v)=d\mathbb T_X(h)+\mathbb T_X(h)d.$$
Every component commutes with the internal differential, and on an input of horizontal degree $n$ the internal terms in this identity are $(-1)^{n-1}d_rE_X(h)+(-1)^nE_X(h)d_r=0$. Consequently chain homotopy equivalences give natural total cochain homotopy equivalences and induced natural isomorphisms in $D(\mathcal C)$ [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. All matrix entries are finite integral sums and all total-degree sums are finite; no infinite coproducts in $\mathcal C$ are required. For diagrams concentrated in internal degree zero the same assertions give evaluation in $\mathcal C$.

proof.text:
Apply [lem-galois-yoneda-hom-bijection] to the category $I^{\mathrm{op}}$ and the underlying set functor of $R_j:I\to\mathrm{Ab}$. Restricting an abelian-group natural transformation $a:R_i\to R_j$ to the generators gives a set-valued transformation $\operatorname{Hom}_I(i,-)\to R_j$, determined by $z=a_i([1_i])$. Conversely, if $z=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha[\alpha]\in R_j(i)$, define
$$a_t([f:i\to t])=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha[f\alpha]$$
and extend by integer linearity to finite formal sums. This extension is unique; for $g:t\to t'$ both naturality composites send $[f]$ to $\sum c_\alpha[gf\alpha]$, so it is natural. Thus the displayed finite coefficient family is unique. For lists $A=(i_a)$ and $B=(j_b)$, use the canonical inclusions and projections of their pointwise finite direct sums. A transformation $M:A\to B$ is uniquely determined by $M_{ba}=\pi_bM\iota_a:R_{i_a}\to R_{j_b}$, since $M=\sum_{a,b}\iota_bM_{ba}\pi_a$. This also covers empty lists, when the morphism is zero.

source.place: Tag 001P, categories-lemma-yoneda; free abelian extension and finite-sum identities written out

proof.text:
The abelian hypothesis [def-sp-abelian] supplies abelian groups of morphisms, bilinear composition and finite biproducts. For a singleton entry $a:R_i\to R_j$ represented by $\sum c_\alpha[\alpha]$, set $e_X(a)=\sum c_\alpha X(\alpha):X(j)\to X(i)$. This is a finite sum of cochain maps, hence a cochain map: its commutation equation with each differential is the sum of those for the $X(\alpha)$. If $b:R_j\to R_k$ is represented by $\sum d_\beta[\beta]$, Step 1 gives
$$ (ba)_i([1_i])=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_\alpha d_\beta[\alpha\beta]. $$
Bilinearity and $X(\alpha\beta)=X(\alpha)X(\beta)$ give $e_X(ba)=e_X(a)e_X(b)$. The coefficient family of the identity is $[1_i]$, so its evaluation is the identity; addition of coefficient families gives $e_X(a+a')=e_X(a)+e_X(a')$. These equations establish all singleton functor laws, including negative and zero coefficients.

source.place: Tag 00ZY, homology-definition-preadditive; explicit finite integral composition calculation

proof.text: Put $E_X(A)=\bigoplus_aX(i_a)$ with componentwise differential. Define $E_X(M):E_X(B)\to E_X(A)$ by the block from $X(j_b)$ to $X(i_a)$ being $e_X(M_{ba})$. For $N:B\to C$, the $(c,a)$ entry of $NM$ is $\sum_bN_{cb}M_{ba}$. By Step 2 its evaluation is $\sum_be_X(M_{ba})e_X(N_{cb})$, exactly the $(a,c)$ block of $E_X(M)E_X(N)$. The biproduct relations $\pi_a\iota_b=\delta_{ab}$ and $\sum_a\iota_a\pi_a=1$ therefore prove contravariant composition, the identity law and additivity. The empty list is sent to zero; the identity of zero is its zero map. If $\tau:X\to Y$ is a natural transformation, its components satisfy $\tau_iX(\alpha)=Y(\alpha)\tau_j$ for $\alpha:j\to i$. Multiply by each coefficient and add: the maps $\bigoplus_a\tau_{i_a}$ give $E_X(A)\to E_Y(A)$ commuting with every evaluated matrix. Their identities and compositions hold componentwise. Thus $E$ is natural in $X$, also on internal differentials.

source.place: Tag 00ZY, homology-definition-preadditive; finite biproduct identities and naturality calculation

proof.text:
For a chain complex $P$, take $d_H^{n,r}=E_X(\partial_{P,n+1})^r:E_X(P_n)^r\to E_X(P_{n+1})^r$ and $d_V=d_r$. Contravariance gives $d_H^2=E_X(\partial_{P,n+1}\partial_{P,n+2})=0$, and $d_V^2=0$. Each evaluated differential is a cochain map by Steps 2–3, so $d_Hd_V=d_Vd_H$. These are exactly the commuting-double-complex conditions of [def-sp-double-complex-total], after extending by zero outside $n,r\geq0$. Its total has the required finite sums and differential. Explicitly, on a summand of bidegree $(n,r)$ its square is
$$d_H^2+(-1)^{n+1}d_Vd_H+(-1)^nd_Hd_V+d_V^2=0.$$
There are only $m+1$ summands in total degree $m\geq0$ and none for $m<0$. Finite biproducts of $\mathcal C$ suffice.

For a chain map $u:P\to Q$, take the bidegree-preserving maps $U^{n,r}=E_X(u_n)^r:E_X(Q_n)^r\to E_X(P_n)^r$. The equation $\partial_{Q,n+1}u_{n+1}=u_n\partial_{P,n+1}$ evaluates to $d_{H,P}U^{n,r}=U^{n+1,r}d_{H,Q}$, and the internal commutation equation gives $d_{V,P}U^{n,r}=U^{n,r+1}d_{V,Q}$. Thus the finite direct sum of these maps commutes separately with the two signed parts of the total differential. It is $\mathbb T_X(u)$. Its contravariant identity and composition laws hold on each summand by Step 3. The same summand equations for $\tau:X\to Y$ show that these cochain maps are natural in $X$.

proof.text:
Suppose $u_n-v_n=\partial_{Q,n+1}h_n+h_{n-1}\partial_{P,n}$, with $h_{-1}=0$. Define $H$ on the total summand $(k,r)$ of $\mathbb T_X(Q)$ by $H^{k,r}=E_X(h_{k-1})^r$ into $(k-1,r)$ of $\mathbb T_X(P)$ when $k\geq1$, and by zero when $k=0$. Thus $H$ has total degree $-1$. On this summand the horizontal contributions to $d_PH+Hd_Q$ are
$$E_X(\partial_{P,k})E_X(h_{k-1})+E_X(h_k)E_X(\partial_{Q,k+1})
=E_X(h_{k-1}\partial_{P,k}+\partial_{Q,k+1}h_k)=E_X(u_k-v_k).$$
The vertical contributions land in $(k-1,r+1)$ and are
$$(-1)^{k-1}d_VE_X(h_{k-1})+(-1)^kE_X(h_{k-1})d_V=0,$$
because $E_X(h_{k-1})$ is an internal cochain map. For $k=0$ both vertical terms and the first horizontal term are absent; the second horizontal term is precisely $E_X(\partial_{Q,1}h_0)=E_X(u_0-v_0)$. These computations on all summand inclusions prove the total homotopy identity. Step 3 applied to the entries of $h$ proves that $H$ is natural in $X$.

source.place: Cochain homotopy equation preceding homology-lemma-compose-homotopy-cochain; explicit signed total calculation

proof.text: Given a chain homotopy inverse $w:Q\to P$ of $u$, Steps 5–6 apply to the two homotopies $wu\simeq1_P$ and $uw\simeq1_Q$. Contravariance identifies their evaluated composites with $\mathbb T_X(u)\mathbb T_X(w)$ and $\mathbb T_X(w)\mathbb T_X(u)$, respectively. Hence these are mutually inverse total cochain homotopy equivalences, natural in $X$. Apply clause (b) of [lem-weil-pbc-homotopic-maps-equal-cohomology] with the identity additive functor: the two composites induce identity maps on every cohomology object, so the two induced cohomology maps are inverse. Therefore $\mathbb T_X(u)$ is a quasi-isomorphism. The localization defining $D(\mathcal C)$ in [def-weil-abstract-derived-category] sends it to an isomorphism, and applying the localization functor to the naturality squares preserves naturality. All sums used above are finite coefficient supports, finite list indices or finite antidiagonals. If $X(i)$ is concentrated in internal degree zero, its only surviving total summand has $r=0$ and $n=m$; all the formulas specialize to the stated evaluation in $\mathcal C$.
